newsitem.title: BULGARIA: New Bulgarian president holds key to crisis.
newsitem.headline: New Bulgarian president holds key to crisis.

text.p: Petar Stoyanov, sworn in on Sunday as Bulgaria's new president, holds the key to breaking a political deadlock over the ruling Socialists' desire to hold on to power and opposition demands for early elections.
"Bulgaria wants elections as soon as possible, Bulgaria must get these elections," the 44-year-old divorce lawyer told parliament on Sunday.

Stoyanov burst on to the political scene in June when he defeated President Zhelyu Zhelev in a U.S.-style primary election aimed to pick a single presidential candidate for the fractious anti-communist opposition.

Tall, athletic and bespectacled, he scored a resounding victory in November's presidential elections. Stoyanov owes his meteoric political rise to Bulgaria's deep economic malaise and the anti-communist opposition's new-found unity.
Virtually unknown outside his Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) party eight months ago, Stoyanov won around 60 percent of the vote, trouncing Ivan Marazov of the governing Socialist Party (BSP).

Under Bulgaria's post-communist constitution, the presidency is a largely ceremonial post but the scale of Stoyanov's victory led to the resignation of Socialist Prime Minister Zhan Videnov at a party congress on December 21.
Massive protests organised by the opposition in the past 13 days have also forced the ruling Socialists to concede to holding fresh elections before the end of the year.

Stoyanov has said he wants the Socialists and opposition to negotiate on an interim administration, but if agreement cannot be found he will reluctantly give the Socialists the new ruling mandate denied them by his predecessor Zhelev.

Bulgarians, impoverished by soaring inflation, a collapsing currency, bank closures and fears of bread and fuel shortages this winter, have threatened to step up nationwide protests and strikes if the Socialists form a second cabinet.

Stoyanov made his pro-market, liberal views clear on Sunday. "I will seek an agreement for urgent economic measures. People are poor because there have been no reforms and this should be understood by the politicians," he said.

Referring to planned aid from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, which will only be handed over after a new government is formed and on condition a tough monetary regime is imposed, he warned that salvation would hurt.
"Elections (will) bring more consensus into society, elections which will let the new rulers, together with the people flooding the streets, carry out the painful but vital economic reforms."

The new president strongly supports binding Bulgaria more closely to Western Europe. The small Balkan country has continued looking towards Moscow, its historic patron, even since the fall of communism.

"We have to make the right choice, which is the European type of civilisation, to show our will and to build the conditions for our integration into the European Union and NATO," Stoyanov said in his inaugural speech.
He made pre-election visits to Germany, where he met Chancellor Helmut Kohl, and to Poland, whose increasing prosperity under a moderate leftist government contrasts strongly with Bulgaria's turmoil.

A professional politician, Stoyanov offers a younger, slicker image than Zhelev, a former dissident academic who always looked slightly ill at ease in a suit. His vigorous, straightforward speech contrasts with Zhelev's rambling, philosophical style.

Zhelev, also a liberal, bowed out of the contest last year. He will formally hand over the keys of office on January 22, in the first ever transfer of office from one elected Bulgarian president to another.
Stoyanov was a victim of a tear gas attack when protesters stormed parliament on January 10 after Socialist deputies refused to approve opposition demands for early elections.
He has made a particular effort to appeal to young voters and has been endorsed by Bulgaria's international soccer stars Hristo Stoichkov and Emil Kostadinov.
Born on May 25, 1952, in Plovdiv, he studied law at Sofia University. He practised law in Plovdiv and became deputy justice minister in the UDF government from 1991 to 1992.

A former volleyball player, he is married with two children. His wife, Antonina Stoyanova, also a lawyer by training, was a diplomat at the Bulgarian embassy in London and returned to Sofia after her husband became president.
